findings.title: canManage() grants manage access to users with only VIEW permission
findings.body: The no-arg `canManage()` method checks for both `AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW` and `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE` scopes: `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. This means a user who only has VIEW permission on all groups will pass `requireManage()`, which is called by `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()`. Such a user would be able to create new top-level groups despite only having view permission. The VIEW scope should be removed from this check, leaving only MANAGE.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() adds authorization resource ID instead of group ID
findings.body: In `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, the code adds `groupResource.getId()` (the internal authorization resource ID) to the `granted` set. However, this set is consumed by `UsersResource.searchForUser()` and `UsersResource.getUsersCount()` as actual group IDs (set via `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` and passed to `getUsersCount` overloads). Since the authorization resource ID is not the same as the group ID, user filtering by group membership will silently fail to match any users. The code should use `groupResource.getName()` instead, which holds the group ID as set by `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup()`.

findings.title: getResourceName does not handle GROUPS resource type
findings.body: The `getResourceName` method has explicit handling for `USERS` resource type (resolving user ID to username) but no handling for `GROUPS` resource type. When a policy references a specific group resource, the method falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which may return null or an unhelpful value since group resources are created with the group ID as the name and no display name is set. This could result in poor UI representation of group resources in permission listings.
